source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, Glaser (1989) Self-explanations: How students study and use examples in learning to solve problems (design and headline result, read via Chi 1994 and VanLehn 1992)
finding: Founding study. Eight college students first read the prose of a physics chapter, then talked aloud on three worked examples, then solved problems. The 4 best problem solvers (Good) had spontaneously produced many more self-explanations than the 4 weaker ones (Poor). This is the self-explanation effect. It is a correlation between spontaneous explaining and later score, not an experiment.
numbers: N=8 (4 Good, 4 Poor), 3 examples. Posttest 82% vs 46% correct. Explanations per example: 15.3 vs 2.8 (as Chi 1994 reports) or 15.5 vs 2.7 (as VanLehn 1992 reports). The two secondary reports differ slightly.
limits: The original PDF at ASU is a scanned image with no text layer; I could not read it. Every number here is taken from Chi 1994 and VanLehn et al 1992, which I did read. Tiny N. Groups were split after the fact by outcome, so ability and prior knowledge are confounded with explaining.
agent_relevance: The effect was first seen as a difference between people who explain a step to themselves and people who only read it. For the agent this suggests that an explicit per-step explanation slot is what separates good from poor study of a worked example.

source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, Glaser (1989) Self-explanations: How students study and use examples in learning to solve problems (self-monitoring and example look-up findings)
finding: Good solvers monitored their own understanding accurately. Poor solvers said they understood when their later performance showed they did not. Good solvers also went back to the examples less often and more precisely while solving.
numbers: Good solvers: 53% of monitoring statements positive, 46% negative. Poor solvers said they understood 85% of the time. Example look-ups per problem: Good 2.7 times, 1.6 lines per look-up; Poor 6.7 times, 13.0 lines per look-up (start at the top and reread). Both groups consulted examples on most problems (about 75% vs 83%).
limits: Figures quoted second-hand from VanLehn, Jones and Chi (1992), who summarise Chi 1989. N=8. The original was unreadable (scanned).
agent_relevance: Poor self-assessment ('okay, that makes sense' when it does not) is the human twin of a model grading its own answer. It supports G2/G3: understanding claims need a check, not the learner's word. Targeted look-up (a few lines, aimed at a gap) is the pattern to copy for memory retrieval.

source: Chi, de Leeuw, Chiu, LaVancher (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (prompted vs unprompted groups)
finding: First controlled test. Eighth graders read a circulatory-system text. One group was asked to explain after every line; the control read the text twice. Prompted students gained more, mostly on hard inference questions.
numbers: 14 prompted vs 10 control. Pre-to-post gain 32% vs 22% (group x test interaction F(1,22)=5.1, p<.05). On the hard Category 3 and 4 questions: +22.6% vs +12.5%, t(22)=2.64, p<.01. Time on task: prompted mean 2h05 (range 1h27 to 2h53); control mean 1h06 (range 22 min to 2h47).
quote: merely asked to self-explain after reading each line of a passage
limits: Time on task was not equal: prompted students spent about twice as long, even though the control read twice. No main effect of group. Small N. Some control students probably explained covertly (2 of 10 drew 21 and 17 diagrams). Ability (CAT scores 87% vs 83%, ns) did not predict gain, t(21)=1.479, p=.15; the prompt effect stayed, t(21)=2.147, p<.05.
agent_relevance: A one-line prompt, with no training, was enough to raise inference learning. This is the evidence base for a cheap 'explain this step' slot in S5. The time confound is a warning: part of the gain may simply be more compute per step.

source: Chi et al. (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (high vs low explainers, open-book look-ups)
finding: Inside the prompted group, students who produced more explanations learned more and understood more deeply. High explainers rarely needed to look back at the text. Dose-response in explanation count.
numbers: Top 4 vs bottom 4 explainers: 87 vs 29 explanation inferences (t(6)=5.64, p<.001); correct ones 61 vs 14. Gain 38% vs 27% (t(6)=2.14, p<.07). Hard questions gain 33% vs 17% (t(6)=3.02, p<.05). Open-book look-ups: 2 vs 11 of 54 posttest questions. Gain after excluding looked-up answers: 37% vs 15% (t(6)=3.22, p<.02).
limits: Only 4 vs 4 students; the 2 lowest were dropped. The split is by the outcome-related quantity itself, so it is correlational inside the group. Overall gain difference was only a trend (p<.07).
agent_relevance: Quantity of useful inferences, not just having a prompt, tracked learning. A single-line explanation per step may be too thin; the signal to measure is inferences that go beyond the stated text.

source: Chi et al. (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (mental-model analysis)
finding: Students' mental models of the circulatory system were coded before and after. Prompted students and high explainers reached the correct 'double loop-2' model far more often.
numbers: Prompted: 8 of 14 (57%) reached double loop-2. Unprompted: 2 of 9 (22%; one student who started at double loop-2 was excluded). High explainers 4 of 4 (100%) vs low explainers 1 of 4 (25%). Across all 24, initial models were 21% no loop and 50% single loop.
limits: Small cells; model coding is subjective (the authors say so). Counts come from the running text; the table in the PDF text layer was garbled.
agent_relevance: The benefit is a repaired internal model, not recall. This matches the aim of S5: name what is wrong so the model can be repaired, not just restated.

source: Chi et al. (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (what the explanations are made of)
finding: Many self-explanations bring in prior knowledge. About one quarter were wrong, yet wrong ones did not hurt learning. The authors argue wrong explanations get contradicted by later text and then repaired.
numbers: At least 30% of explanations integrated new text with prior (often common-sense) knowledge. About 25% of explanations were incorrect, in both the physics data and this study; results were unchanged when incorrect ones were partialed out. Ability did not matter: 5 highest-CAT (mean 98%) and 5 lowest-CAT (72%) explainers both gained about 30%.
quote: generating incorrect self-explanations was not detrimental to learning
limits: The repair story is an interpretation; it was not tested directly. The text was well written and always correct, so contradiction was guaranteed. With no correct source (as in an LLM loop with no checker) wrong explanations may not get repaired.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: a wrong explanation is useful only because something real later contradicts it. For the agent that something must be code output or a held-out check, not another sample from the same model.

source: Chi et al. (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (three-characteristic account)
finding: The theory. Self-explaining works because it is (1) constructive, (2) integrative with prior knowledge, and (3) piecemeal, so conflicts with the evolving model get noticed and repaired. Summarising, diagram drawing and writing a complete theory-based explanation each lack one of these.
numbers: Cited support: VanLehn, Jones and Chi (1992) found only 50-60% of the rules needed for the physics problems were in the text, so the rest had to be constructed. Authors suggest micro, partial explanations repair misconceptions better than complete theory-based ones.
limits: A conceptual account, not a tested mechanism. The summarising claim is a prediction.
agent_relevance: Design hint for S5: ask for a small, local explanation of one step against what the model already believes, not a grand rationale. Fits the 'one-line naming' idea.

source: VanLehn, Jones, Chi (1992) A model of the self-explanation effect (Cascade): the human data it explains
finding: Summary of the three protocol studies behind the effect (Chi 1989 physics; Pirolli and Bielaczyc 1989 LISP; Fergusson-Hessler and de Jong 1990 mass spectrometer). Good solvers differ from Poor in four ways: more self-explanations, more accurate monitoring, fewer example look-ups, and more targeted look-ups.
numbers: Pirolli and Bielaczyc: Good solvers spent 45% of episodes on deep processing vs 18% for Poor; Poor spent 19% on superficial study vs 10%. 'Everything is clear' appeared three times more in Poor protocols (Fergusson-Hessler and de Jong). In problem solving, Chi, VanLehn and Reiner (1988) found the Poor solver had 30 impasses in 77 episodes (39%) and the Good solver 7 in 31 (23%); in 6 of the Good solver's 7 impasses a correct piece of knowledge was learned.
limits: Three small protocol studies; the impasse comparison is a single Good and a single Poor solver.
agent_relevance: Impasses are where learning happens, and Poor solvers learn wrong things at impasses. This supports G1 (react to an impasse signal) and the need for a check before keeping a lesson.

source: VanLehn, Jones, Chi (1992) A model of the self-explanation effect (Cascade): mechanism and simulations
finding: Cascade is a rule-based simulation (Prolog rules over physics examples). Explaining an example gives two kinds of knowledge: domain rules, learned when an impasse is resolved with an overly general rule that is then specialised, and derivational knowledge, which later guides search by analogy. A Good-solver run derives every example line; the Poor-solver run only reads the lines.
numbers: Run 1 (explain + analogy): 8 rules learned while studying examples, 15 while solving, 23 total; 23 of 23 problems solved. Run 2 (no explaining): 3 rules, 9 problems solved; 6 problems got a wrong answer; 8 failed or timed out at 20 min. Run 3 (explain, no analogical search control): 18 rules, 4 of them incorrect; 19 problems solved. The authors conclude the learning mechanisms are jointly sufficient to reproduce the effect and neither alone does.
limits: A simulation of 3 examples and 23 problems, tuned to reproduce known protocols. It shows sufficiency, not that people actually learn this way. Run 4 detail was not captured in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: A formal account that matches the schema's logic: derive a step, find where the derivation breaks, fix the rule at that point, keep the derivation to steer later search. This is close to storing a derivation (subgoal library) rather than only an answer.

source: Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi, Winne (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis (overall effect)
finding: Prompting or directing learners to self-explain gives a moderate gain over comparison conditions, with real spread across studies.
numbers: 69 effect sizes from 64 reports, 5,917 participants. Random effects g = .552 (SE .050, 95% CI .454 to .650). Heterogeneity Q=196.63, df=68, p<.001; I2 = 65.4%. Fail-safe N 6,028; Orwin fail-safe 274 null studies to bring g under 0.1.
limits: Most comparisons are prompted vs unprompted, so this is about induced self-explanation, not the spontaneous explaining of Chi 1989. Authors note time on task was rarely reported or equated. Publication-bias tests are weak ones.
agent_relevance: Gives a defensible prior: about half a standard deviation for a prompt, not a miracle. Expect smaller gains once compute is matched.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) meta-analysis: effect by comparison condition
finding: The size of the effect depends on what it is compared against. Against no explanation it is largest. Against a ready-made instructional explanation or another strategy it is about half as big.
numbers: No additional explanation: g=.673, k=41, N=3,141. Instructional explanation: g=.354, k=6, N=573 (CI .175 to .533). Other strategy: g=.304, k=7, N=516. Mixed: g=.462, k=15, N=1,687. Test of difference QB=11.65, df=3, p=.009.
limits: Only 6 studies directly compare self- with instructional explanation. Authors read the .35 result as against the 'coverage' hypothesis (that explaining only adds missing information) but concede much of the benefit can also be supplied by an instructor.
agent_relevance: If a good explanation is given by a stronger source (a checker, a trace, a retrieved lesson), a model's own explanation adds less. Compare own-explanation against provided-explanation in any test.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) meta-analysis: effect by learning task and subject
finding: Self-explanation helps in every task type but the gain is not equal. Studying a worked example, the paradigm of Chi 1989, shows one of the smaller gains. Text study is largest.
numbers: Study text: g=.787, k=14, N=772. Solve problems: g=.476, k=20, N=1,415. Study worked examples: g=.362, k=8, N=649, CI .109 to .615. Study cases .432 (k=4); simulation .241 (k=2, not significant). Task-type test QB=10.15, df=6, p=.119 (not significant). Subjects: science .565 (k=25), math .441 (k=16), social science .555 (k=6), computer science .761 (k=9).
limits: Task-type differences were not statistically significant. Small k in several cells.
agent_relevance: For procedure-like material (worked examples, code) the gain is modest. Do not expect large gains on every ARC-style item.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) meta-analysis: effect by prompt type and test format
finding: Prompt form matters little, with some exceptions. Multiple-choice prompts and metacognitive prompts (explain your plan or performance) showed no reliable effect. Essay-format outcomes also showed no reliable effect.
numbers: Multiple-choice prompts g=.24 (k=2, not significant). Metacognitive prompts not significant; conceptual prompts better than metacognitive (z=3.28, p=.001). Anticipatory prompts g=1.37 but k=1. Justify own decision g=.42, justify another's .43. Essay outcomes g=.624, k=3, CI -.185 to 1.433.
limits: k=1 and k=2 cells carry little weight. The authors only speculate that strong cues in multiple-choice prompts undercut generation.
agent_relevance: Prompts should ask for content-level 'why does this step follow' rather than 'how am I doing'. Fits S5 naming what is wrong in the content itself.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) meta-analysis: region effect and on-demand explanations
finding: East Asian studies reported much larger effects than North American or European ones, which the authors treat as unexplained heterogeneity. They also report that offering instructional explanations on request did not help over self-explanation alone.
numbers: East Asia g=1.191 (k=6, N=456) vs North America .525 (k=42, N=3,456) and Europe .481 (k=18, N=1,791); QB=13.14, df=4, p=.011. Schworm and Renkl (2006), as cited: self-explanation prompts alone beat prompts plus on-demand instructional explanations.
limits: The region effect may reflect design or measurement differences, not culture. The Schworm and Renkl result is cited from the meta-analysis, not read in the original.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that handing over the answer or a hint too early removes the incentive to generate. Matches the schema's reluctance to reveal answers early.

source: Bichler, Stadler, Buhner, Greiff, Fischer (2026) Worked examples, cognitive aptitudes and the self-explanation mechanism: a replication
finding: A replication of a study on whether self-explanation quality mediates the worked-example effect. The original found no mediation; the replication, with stronger methods, found mediation, but only for some learners.
numbers: N=115 university students, six ill-defined statistics problems, with or without worked examples. Moderated mediation via self-explanation quality for prior knowledge and working-memory capacity, with stronger indirect effects at lower aptitude. Not moderated by fluid intelligence. No mediation for shifting ability.
limits: Read as an abstract only (via Europe PMC), not the full paper. Mediation analyses from one lab; quality coded by raters.
agent_relevance: Self-explanation is not the only route by which examples help; it matters most for low-resource learners. For the agent, examples may help directly without explanation when the model is already strong.

source: Scheitz, Hollmann, Nemeth, Lipowsky, Ferri, Osterberg (2025) Interleaving subtraction strategies goes solo: no added benefit from initial blocking or self-explanation
finding: A null result for self-explanation prompts. Adding prompts to interleaved practice gave no further gain, though self-explanation quality predicted outcomes.
numbers: N=238 third graders, 3 x 2 design, tests before, right after, and at 8 and 16 weeks. Interleaving beat blocked practice on flexibility, adaptivity and conditional strategy knowledge for up to 16 weeks. Self-explanation prompts vs extra practice: no added benefit. Quality of explanation still predicted short-term adaptivity, accuracy and conditional knowledge, and conditional knowledge at 8 and 16 weeks.
limits: Preprint, abstract only for me. Deductive instruction in elementary arithmetic; the control got extra practice (time matched).
agent_relevance: A prompt effect can vanish when time is matched and another strong method is present. Quality predicts; the mere presence of a prompt does not. Do not credit the slot, credit its content.

source: McGinn, Booth, Huyghe (2025) Preparing 4th and 5th graders to learn algebra with worked examples and self-explanation prompts
finding: A large classroom trial of MathByExample (worked examples plus self-explanation prompts) found no overall benefit. Benefits appeared only for students who did many prompts and had enough prior knowledge.
numbers: 58 US classrooms, randomised by classroom, year-long. No significant overall effect on foundational algebra knowledge (FAK) or on preparation for future learning (PFL). More self-explanation attempts helped FAK only with a high number of worksheets; self-explanation attempts improved PFL only for students with at least average prior knowledge. Higher-prior-knowledge students were hurt by more worksheets.
limits: Abstract only for me. The moderators are post-hoc dosage analyses, so they are correlational.
agent_relevance: A real-world failure at scale: prompts need uptake and a learner who can produce something to say. A weak model that cannot generate a correct explanation may gain nothing.

source: Yip et al. (2026) Cultivating reasoning through example-based or self-explanation-based teaching (CREST)? Medical Science Educator
finding: A small randomised comparison where self-explanation lost to a worked demonstration for novices. Authors read it through cognitive load theory.
numbers: 27 second-year medical students with no ophthalmology knowledge: example-based teaching n=15, self-explanation n=12. Day 10 clinical reasoning median 54.63 vs 48.15 (p=.047); germane load 76.17 vs 71.25 (p=.016). No difference at day 40.
limits: Tiny N, medians, one topic, masked grader. Gap closed by day 40. Authors call for larger studies.
agent_relevance: Novices without prior knowledge can lose from having to self-explain. Matches the expertise-reversal logic from earlier documents in this series: an explanation slot is not free when the base knowledge is missing.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice less, explain more: LLM-supported self-explanation improves explanation quality on transfer problems in calculus
finding: Randomised test of LLM feedback on students' free-text self-explanations in a calculus tutor, fixed 60-minute session. No difference in ordinary posttest score. Better explanation quality only on 'not enough information' transfer items.
numbers: N=92 (Prolific adults; 301 recruited, 104 dropped): control n=29, menu-based n=35, open-ended with LLM feedback n=28. Open-ended vs control on NEI transfer explanations: +11.9 points, SE 5.8, t=2.06, p=.030, 95% CI 1.2 to 22.6, d=0.44. Menu-based +4.7, p=.343. All-explanation measure +7.3%, p=.057, d=0.38. NEI multiple choice +9.3%, p=.183, d=0.26. Pre-to-post gain +9.4% (open) vs +9.3% (control). Practice problems done: 58.9 (control) vs 16.9 (open-ended).
limits: One outcome of several is significant, with no correction mentioned; underpowered; online adults, high attrition. Authors cite Matthews and Rittle-Johnson and McEldoon et al. as finding self-explanation advantages vanish when controls practise more in the same time.
agent_relevance: With time held fixed, doing about a third as many problems gave equal learning. Evidence that explanation can be worth its cost, and that feedback on the explanation (a checker) is what makes open-ended explaining pay.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan, Hassany, Akhuseyinoglu, Hendrawan, Brusilovsky (2026) Self-explanation tutor for active study of CS1 worked examples (ESSE)
finding: An LLM judges students' explanations of Java example lines and returns correctness and completeness feedback. Against a domain expert the LLM is precise but under-credits correct explanations. Students revised when told something was missing.
numbers: Deployment: 8 students, 409 attempts, 358 expert-rated attempts. Correctness vs expert: precision .95, recall .87, F1 .91, accuracy 83.8%, but chance-corrected agreement kappa=.32; 42 false negatives vs 16 false positives (McNemar p=.001). Completeness score vs expert label: point-biserial .39, AUC .67, mean absolute error .45. Revision rate 63% after an incorrect verdict vs 35% after a correct one; mean 1.66 attempts per explanation; 38% got a second attempt (83 of 216). Completeness rose across attempts (Wilcoxon r=.84, p<.001), driven by added concepts more than words. Only 3 of 8 took the posttest; normalised gains .67, -.25, .78.
limits: Pilot with 8 students; learning evidence is anecdotal. A crowd-rater comparison was also run but not extracted here.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge of explanations is only fairly reliable (kappa .32) and leans harsh. That fits G5: a model judge's score is a hint. The revision pattern (revise exactly when a gap is flagged) is the behaviour S5 wants.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan, Hassany, Brusilovsky (2026) Exploring the effectiveness of using LLMs for automated assessment of student self-explanations in programming education
finding: On a balanced set of student code explanations, an LLM judge with a rubric prompt scored far above semantic-similarity methods at deciding if an explanation is correct.
numbers: LLM (behavior prompt): F1 0.98, accuracy 0.96. Semantic similarity baselines: RoBERTa F1 0.70 / accuracy 0.61; Deep Tutor F1 0.69 / accuracy 0.60; best similarity F1 0.72 / accuracy 0.65. 5-fold cross-validation on a balanced set of 1,435 positive and 1,435 negative examples.
limits: Balanced classes, one dataset, binary label. The same group's deployed result (a20) gives F1 .91 and kappa .32 against a single expert on skewed real data, so 0.98 is likely a ceiling.
agent_relevance: LLM graders of explanations look excellent on balanced benchmarks and merely fair when classes are skewed. Test any critic on realistic, skewed data before trusting it.

source: Gao, Lin, Li, Yang, Wu, Ma, Li (2023) Self-explanation prompting improves dialogue understanding in large language models
finding: Zero-shot prompt that tells the model to explain each dialogue utterance before answering. It improved task-oriented dialogue results and matched or beat few-shot prompts. The authors cite Chi 1989 as motivation: not every explanation helps, content and depth matter.
numbers: Six datasets (MultiWOZ 2.1, SGD, SpokenWOZ, STARv2, MELD, MuTual). Gain of about 12 points on STARv2. Ablation on MultiWOZ 2.1 joint goal accuracy with gpt-3.5-turbo: vanilla 35.93; 'first understand' 36.52; 'first summarize' 40.98; explain every utterance 44.44. Chain-of-thought did not help the dialogue tasks. Gains on emotion recognition and response selection were modest.
limits: Prompt-engineering paper; one backbone in the ablation; not a test of the learner effect. The authors do not test whether explanations are faithful. Emotion tasks gained little.
agent_relevance: Closest direct use of the idea in LLMs: a structured per-step explanation beat a vague 'understand first' prompt (+0.6) and a summary (+5.1). Structure of the explanation matters, not the label 'explain'.

source: Zhao, Yao, Yang, Yu (2024) Large language models are in-context teachers for knowledge reasoning (Self-Explain)
finding: The model writes its own rationales for training questions and uses them as few-shot examples. This beat human-written rationales and auto-CoT on knowledge reasoning. The idea is tied to encoding specificity, and the paper cites Chi et al. 1989.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo test accuracy (MedMCQA / MedQA / StrategyQA): Self-Explain 56.6 / 59.6 / 59.7; Human CoT 53.2 / 57.5 / 58.5; Auto-CoT 53.1 / 55.6 / 56.1; zero-shot CoT 52.5 / 55.2 / 52.7; no CoT 51.7 / 52.1 / 46.8. Rationales generated given the right answer vs a wrong answer: 56.6 / 59.6 / 59.7 vs 56.0 / 59.4 / 59.1.
limits: Differences of 1 to 3 points, no error bars in the table as extracted; one model for the headline table. The finding is about exemplar style (self-generated), not about a learner's gain. Rationales conditioned on the wrong answer are only 0.2 to 0.6 points worse.
agent_relevance: A model's own explanations make better stored examples than outside ones. Relevant to the lesson store: keep lessons in the model's own words. Also, an explanation need not be right to help as an exemplar.

source: Zhou, Li, Zhang, Leqi (2025) ExPO: Unlocking hard reasoning with self-explanation-guided reinforcement learning (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: When RL cannot find any correct sample on hard problems, the model is asked to explain the known right answer, and that explanation is used as a positive sample. It beats expert-written chain-of-thought as guidance because it is closer to the model's own distribution.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, MATH test by level, pass@4: ExP-GRPO 96/91/86/76/23 percent (levels 1 to 5); GRPO with ground-truth expert CoT SFT 95/89/83/65/12; GRPO 91/84/77/39 (levels 1 to 4). Base pass@128 on level 5 is 4%. Level-5 test set has 1,324 questions. Also tested on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and GSM8K.
limits: Training-time method; it changes weights, which our scaffold does not. One table, no seeds visible. Answer-conditioned explanations are rationalisation and can bake in a wrong path.
agent_relevance: Shows explanation conditioned on a known-correct result is useful signal. Our analogue is explaining a failing output against the true expected output (G2), not explaining unprompted.

source: Lee, MacLellan, Weitekamp (2026) Structure-mapping-guided self-explanation for learning mathematical procedures
finding: A computational model of self-explanation from worked examples. Instead of testing every combination of numbers and operations, it maps parts of the earlier expression onto the changed result and searches near those anchors first. Naive self-explanation search is combinatorially explosive.
numbers: 70 mathematical transformations with 120 changed numeric components. Recovered every intended procedure. Intended procedure returned before any other computation giving the same value in 104 subproblems (86.7%) vs a median of 32 (26.7%) across 100 random-order unguided runs. 93.8% fewer value-operation combinations tested.
limits: Symbolic model on a hand-made set of algebra transformations; no human or LLM data. It is a hypothesis about people, not a fit.
agent_relevance: A computational reading of 'explain the step': abduce which operation produced the change. Anchoring search on structural correspondence is a way to keep a per-step explanation cheap and checkable by code.

source: Fu, Ramasubbu, Galletta (2026) Knowing is not enough: information retrievability as a precondition to effective LLM oversight
finding: People who first wrote their own explanation of why LLM answers were wrong were better at catching LLM errors later than people who only received the standard explanation. A personal retrieval cue slowed the decline over a week.
numbers: Study 1: 407 employees completed (N=400 analysed), system explanation n=204 vs self-explanation n=203. Error detection about 10.6 percentage points higher with self-explanation; false positives 3 points lower; odds of high detection about 3.9 times. Study 2: N=240, baseline plus seven workdays, own cue vs neutral phrase slowed the decline (interaction OR 1.17, p<.001).
limits: Preprint (forthcoming); employees at one firm in China; error detection on email tasks. This is human oversight of LLMs, not an LLM learning.
agent_relevance: Generation before reading the answer is what made the difference, repeating the Bisra result. Supports having the agent commit to its own explanation before it is shown a checker result.

source: Eleftheriou, Pallis, Constantinides (2026) Confidence without competence in AI-assisted knowledge work
finding: Three LLM interaction designs were compared with a standard assistant: future-self explanation, contrastive learning and guided hints. The standard assistant gave the highest perceived and lowest actual learning. Future-self explanation lined up confidence best with real understanding but cost more effort.
numbers: Phase 2 with 85 participants across two tasks (Phase 1 interviews with 16 students). Guided hints gave the largest learning gains; future-self explanations the closest match between perceived and actual understanding and the highest workload. Effect sizes not extracted.
limits: I read the abstract and framing only. HCI study with small cells; 'future-self explanation' is a variant, not the Chi paradigm.
agent_relevance: A fluent complete answer inflates confidence without learning, the same as a poor self-monitor in Chi 1989. Treat model confidence after reading an answer as unreliable.

source: Renkl (1997) Learning from worked-out examples: a study on individual differences (Cognitive Science 21, 1-29)
finding: Follow-up that went deeper on who benefits. Quality of self-explanation, not just amount, predicted learning when time was fixed. Two successful styles: principle-based explaining and anticipative reasoning (predict the next step before seeing it).
numbers: 36 university freshmen studying probability calculus examples individually. Fixed learning time. Success linked to principle-based explanations, anticipative reasoning and explicit operator-goal combinations. Full numbers not obtained.
limits: Read as an abstract and secondary summaries only (search snippet); I could not open the paper. Treat numbers as missing.
agent_relevance: 'Anticipate the next step, then check' is a form of self-explanation a program can do: predict, compare to the real next step, flag the gap (S5). Bisra's single anticipatory study had g=1.37.

source: Scoping reviews of student explanation in mathematics and statistics (arXiv 2508.14417; 2503.19237)
finding: Two scoping reviews list the explanation literature in secondary and postsecondary maths: 41 and 46 studies, covering self-explanation, peer explanation and explaining to fictitious others. Both say explanation builds conceptual and procedural understanding.
numbers: 41 studies (middle and secondary) and 46 studies (postsecondary).
limits: I saw only the arXiv listing summary, not the papers. Scoping reviews do not compute effect sizes.
agent_relevance: A route to the literature on explaining to a fictitious other, adjacent to our one-agent design (agent explains to a self-check).
